And think I thank God there are transcripts, and I objected to this document, if you remember, these are my objections, because two years ago, we were given only this page of the order, and then in the cross-examination, all of a sudden, the second page turned up and the Prosecution alleges that it is part of page 1, but it turned up only during the cross-examination, and a year ago, when we received this first page, it only said end of document. And I have it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, let's just shorten it. What does the witness say? Is that General Praljak's signature or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am really not an expert witness. I cannot resolve this. What I could say is that this isn't the general's signature but on the other hand, it could be. I'd say it isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Certainly hedging your bets on this one, whereas you were quite happy to identify signatures on others, but we can pass on and we will take on board what you all say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry, I'm not trying to evade answering. What I'm saying that it looks like but it on the other hand, it doesn't look like the signature, the general's signature, which I saw when he signed but then again I'm no expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, P576, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same subject, look at what the heading says, who is the commander of the operative zone and what does it say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, the order is issued on behalf of, for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whose signature it is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know whose signature this is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question in principle, when such orders are issued on the front lines, who is authorised to sign them, from what you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander is authorised to sign them. But I'm telling you that I never saw this order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now document P718.1. Tell me, please, people who were with the Croatian Army in 1991 and 1992, could they exercise their rights in the Croatian Army deriving from that? For instance, were they entitled to health care, to ranks, to pensions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'm asking you, I'm not asking about others. Did you also get or could you also exercise your right to a rank in the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I did not apply for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know from your own knowledge whether somebody else applied for it and got a rank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that somebody did apply and they got their ranks. But they would immediately be transferred to the reserve force, and in case of war, that rank could be reactivated and could become active duty but in principle it is a reserve rank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you are a trained soldier, so let us please try to resolve a dilemma. Please help us. What -- those ranks in the HVO, what about them? I'm interested in 1992, 1993. Did you have any ranks or not? When, how? And if you got any ranks, when did you get those ranks and how?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, in 1991, in Croatia, in 1992, in Herceg-Bosna, when we arrived in the HVO, there were no ranks. There were formation duties but -- posts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, explain it to us because we are all laymen? What does that mean? What does that mean, formation posts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means somebody was a commander of a battalion, that would mean either a major or a colonel, it would correspond to this but there were no ranks, although some people addressed those men on the basis of the duties they performed. Sorry, somebody commanded a battalion he would be addressed as a major, of a brigade, brigadier or colonel, and at a lower level, people would say sergeant, staff sergeant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But to make a rank a rank, what is the procedure, please, and when did you get your ranks in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure to get a rank is that the superior command makes such a proposal. In my case, it is the Main Staff. And on the basis, pursuant to this proposal, one gets a rank, depending on the level of that rank, it is signed either by the Supreme Commander for the highest ranks, colonels, brigadiers and generals, and at a lower level, Minister of Defence or chief of the department, head of the department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Must these ranks be published in the Official Gazette, in Narodne Novine, the Official Gazette which carries all the laws?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Official Gazette carries the decree on the rank and only then, that is eight days later that becomes a valid and final rank, is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what -- when it comes into effect but definitely after it has been published by Narodne Novine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was this procedure introduced?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: This procedure was introduced sometime in 1993, I believe, no I'm not quite sure, I told you with dates, you know, don't ask me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But would you know was it the -- in late 1993 or in mid-1993, early?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd say it was the latter half but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move to Exhibit P740.2. Please I saw something added by hand, so I wanted to ask you about that, but I'll ask something else. It says here in the lower right-hand bottom of the document, what does it say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since Her Honour Judge Clark has warned me and I did make a mistake when I intervened, I should not have done that, now I don't know how to put this question to you. I have been thinking long and hard on how to put this question, and I think that this will be a fair way to ask you: Yesterday, on direct, when I asked you whether there were Croatian Army units in Mostar from the Republic of Croatia, at the time, you said that there were -- that there weren't. And now I'm asking you: At that time, in Mostar, do you have any personal knowledge of the Croatian Army, from the Republic of Croatia, being in the area of Herzegovina or Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, there were no Croatian Army units in Herzegovina. There was a number of soldiers who had been in the Croatian Army during the war and who came to fight and defend Herzegovina and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Clark? Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I have three areas of questions and I hope I don't take long with them. Can I ask you, Witness, we have to go into private session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: In total, how much time did you and your unit spend on active duty in Mostar during the period of the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were in Mostar three times, but every time it was two to three days. We would only intervene at the most critical moments. Then we would pull out and other units would arrive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And can I take it that as soon as you performed your critical duty and left, you went to another theatre of conflict? You left the Mostar region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wherever we were, we would carry out our task and we would return to either our base or to some other place, but there were some areas where we stayed longer. When there was not enough troops to hold certain lines reached, with that, I mean home guard units, then it would be our task to hold these lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'm trying to rush you through because of the time constraints. So can I take it that you really spent at the very most maybe six to nine days in the Mostar municipality? Just answer me yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: In that six or nine days, did you only meet Mr. Naletilic once?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: How do you know what his position in the HVO was, then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Mr. Naletilic in April, 1992. And I knew he was the commander of the Convicts Battalion. And later on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Go ahead, I'm very conscious of the time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: And later on, I'm sorry, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You see, witness, I thought you said that you met Mr. Naletilic for the first time on the 9th or 10th of May in Mostar. I thought that's what you said. Now you say you met him in 1992. But, however, we will move on from that. We can check the transcript. The other question I want to ask you about is if we go back to the conflict in Mostar on the 9th and 10th of May, you mentioned that after the surrender of the people in the Vranica building, that you went in there and you conducted a search. Were you with other people in carrying out this search of the building? Again short answers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: About how many of you would have conducted this search?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some 20 of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Very good. Did you particularly conduct a search of the offices of the headquarters of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The basement offices which housed the headquarters of the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I wanted to know. Was it the basement? And were you in charge of that search? Because obviously it was an important one.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can you tell me were there many documents taken and also while you're considering that, was there any evidence that any documents had either been removed or destroyed by the previous occupants of the basement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found a lot of documents but there were also traces that a lot of them had been destroyed. There were traces of ashes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And can you say approximately how many boxes, were there two or three boxes of documents or dozens of boxes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I use this desk as an illustration?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would probably be half full. There were some maps and other things, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, can you answer a question for me as a professional military plan? And we've had very, very few so far. Was -- as far as you know, did the Convicts Battalion have a special purpose unit or was it a special purpose unit? Because it's not clear and it's probably a matter of translation. In other words the Convicts Battalion was a battalion as such, was it one that had included it in a special purpose unit or was the whole battalion a special purpose unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Convicts Battalion was a special battalion but it has never reached its full combat strength.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. And then finally, there is one question in relation to General Bobetko, and you as a senior officer said that or suggested that you wouldn't dare to write General Bobetko directly. What was his position at the end of 1993, 1994, in the Croatian Army? What was his standing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, according to the document that I read, he was the Chief of the Main Staff of the Croatian Army. At the time, I was not even close to the rank of a general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your answers have been extremely helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from Judges' questions? I see none.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one Further examination by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among those documents did you personally see some sort of certificates from -- or thank you notes from Mr. Pasalic and what did these thank you notes refer to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That does not arise out of my questions. If I had referred to the contents of the documents, maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give the evidence, which is a great help to us. When the usher pulls down the blinds, she will take you out of the room. We all wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As for the documents, I understand that both parties have some documents to tender, and as well as some objections to the documents tendered by the other party. I wish that you could submit your written submissions in a few days. Since we are under the time pressure, I think we have to break at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, are we going to sit in Courtroom II tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So we will resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning in Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
